title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, artifact‑grounded study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) to measure the marginal benefit of inserting a deterministic verifier+repair layer (generate→verify→repair, G→V→R) versus accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and produced a single shared generator output per intent (shared_initial_generation) that both arms evaluated. Requested_model = gpt-5-mini. Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The guarded repair pathway was never invoked (repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes). We release the complete preregistration, raw model/provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts (hashes listed in the Disclosure). We interpret the null as a ceiling case under the exact task/model/validator regime and provide concrete design guidance for future confirmatory evaluations that aim to demonstrate verifier/repair utility in more operationally realistic settings.

sections.introduction: Automated intent→configuration translation promises faster and more consistent network change. However, incorrect or out‑of‑order changes can cause outages or functional regressions; accordingly, many architectures pair stochastic generators (LLMs) with deterministic verifiers and repair modules (the generate→verify→repair pattern, G→V→R). Prior work and position papers advocate G→V→R because deterministic checks can (i) detect violations of workflow invariants (e.g., shut before MTU change), (ii) block unsafe applies, and (iii) trigger constrained repairs. Yet published evaluations vary in sampling, task definitions, generator variability, and verifier fidelity. Those differences complicate causal inference about the verifier’s marginal value. To address this, we preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment that isolates the verifier effect by holding the generator output fixed across arms (shared_initial_generation), using deterministic task selection and a deterministic validator. The preregistration and execution artifacts are archived and cryptographically hashed (see Disclosure). Our confirmatory estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded minus baseline).
sections.related_work: Recent literature on LLMs for NetOps and AIOps clusters around three themes: (1) LLM‑based intent translation and configuration synthesis; (2) generate→validate→repair pipelines that integrate formal or emulated validators to assess functional correctness; and (3) agentic orchestration frameworks that coordinate models, skills, and validators in multi‑step workflows. Benchmarks such as Cornetto argue for verifier‑guided iterative workflows to avoid regressions; other position works recommend confining LLMs to translation/translation‑to‑model tasks and relying on solvers for long‑horizon reasoning. Our work complements these strands by providing a preregistered, paired, artifact‑complete causal estimate of the verifier’s marginal effect under a tightly constrained, deterministic regime. We cite the most relevant leads used to form our design (Cornetto and recent position/verification works) and verify them in the literature record supplied with the run.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory framing. The experimental design was preregistered (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop). Key frozen elements: single requested_model (gpt-5-mini), deterministic task sampling from a synthetic pool, deterministic validator semantics (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), shared_initial_generation per task that both arms consume, at most one repair call permitted per guarded episode, and exact analysis code (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Power assumptions were preregistered (target baseline regression rate ≈ 0.20; target absolute reduction 0.08 at α=0.05, 80% power) but the eventual observed baseline differed (see Results). All preregistered parameters, seeds, and analysis code paths are archived (preregistration SHA‑256 = a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622).
Task generation and deterministic sampling. Tasks were drawn deterministically from a public synthetic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Inclusion rules: verifier‑coverage filter, then deterministic selection by SHA‑256(intent_string) sorted ascending; first K=200 tasks selected without human adjudication. Each task manifest entry records the initial_state, expected_final_state, intent, required_sequence, and difficulty metadata. Representative entries and the full task_manifest are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...).
Paired treatment and shared generation. For each task we executed exactly one generator call producing candidate_c (shared_initial_generation). Baseline applied candidate_c as the suggested change; guarded validated candidate_c using deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and invoked a single preregistered repair call only if the validator flagged violations (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). This paired, fixed‑generator design isolates the verifier+repair marginal effect because generator variability is held constant across conditions. Model calls used: 200 shared generations (model_calls_used=200). Provider call traces and per‑call hashes were archived for audit (execution/provider_calls/*.json).
Validator, scoring, and repair. The deterministic validator parses candidate text into structured commands and enforces preregistered workflow invariants (e.g., shutdown before MTU change, minimum‑up constraints). The scoring rule used for the confirmatory outcome was full_intent_constraint_validation. When valid==false the repair policy permits one constrained repair prompt to the same model; repair attempts and repaired candidates are revalidated once. Validator traces capture normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshots, and any violation codes; these per‑episode traces are archived under execution/scoring/ (representative files and hashes are listed in the execution manifest).

sections.discussion:
Interpretation and ceiling effect. The degenerate null result arises because, on this synthetic task pool and with the requested_model (gpt-5-mini) and the deterministic validator, the generator’s shared_initial outputs satisfied all validator constraints. Consequently the verifier had no opportunity to block or repair applies; the trial therefore documents a ceiling regime where G→V→R, as instantiated, yields no observable marginal benefit. This is a valid experimental outcome: a preregistered confirmatory test can legitimately return a null when the assumed baseline error rate differs from the realized baseline.
Design lessons for future evaluations. Demonstrating verifier/repair value in confirmatory frameworks requires a failure‑rich experimental design. From the archived artifacts we derive concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations: (1) use task banks that intentionally sample near the validator’s coverage boundary or include historical failure cases so baseline error > 0; (2) evaluate multiple generator strengths or weaker models to raise baseline failure rates; (3) consider adversarial or perturbed generator outputs to force verifier engagement; or (4) alter the estimand or design to permit interactive generator–verifier exchanges (the current shared_initial_generation design deliberately prevents generator adaptation to verifier feedback and therefore cannot observe benefits that depend on such iterative adaptation). The preregistration explicitly recorded this shared_initial_generation choice and its implications.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: deterministic sampling, seeds, and cryptographic hashing preserve run integrity; all artifacts and execution logs are archived. Construct validity: the primary outcome measures validator.valid; if the validator’s coverage differs from production concerns, the outcome’s operational implication is limited. External validity: the experiment is constrained to one model (gpt-5-mini), a synthetic deterministic task bank, and a single deterministic validator — caution is required before generalizing to production NetOps distributions. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumed baseline failure ≈ 0.20; observed baseline = 1.0 invalidated those power assumptions and transformed the inferential context to an exact null/ceiling case; we therefore report exact tests and bootstrap CIs and avoid claims of equivalence beyond the sampled regime.
Operational implications. Practitioners should not infer from this ceiling case that verifiers are unnecessary in production. Instead the artifacts show how to design reproducible evaluation contracts that diagnose when verifiers are likely to matter. If production task distributions include edge cases, vendor idiosyncrasies, or stateful interactions not captured by the deterministic validator, verifier and repair layers can still provide critical risk reduction.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired study comparing G→V→R against LLM‑only acceptance on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks with a fixed shared generator output per task. Under this constrained regime the verifier never observed failing candidates and therefore produced no marginal effect: both arms achieved 200/200 validator‑compliant applies (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). We release the full artifact bundle (preregistration, raw traces, validator traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts) to enable exact replay. The study documents a ceiling case and provides concrete, artifact‑grounded guidance for future confirmatory evaluations that aim to demonstrate verifier/repair utility in more realistic failure‑rich distributions.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLM families or model strengths without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task bank and deterministic sampling — external validity to production intents, vendor diversity, and operator‑authored change texts is limited.
Construct validity tied to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 coverage: the primary outcome measures validator.valid and thus depends on validator fidelity to operational regressions.
Ceiling effect: observed baseline success = 100% prevented observation of verifier marginal benefit under this design and sample.

Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite deterministic hashing and logging; contamination summary recorded no flagged items but nondetectable overlap remains a general concern.
